stem: A 30-year-old woman with suspected multiple sclerosis undergoes lumbar puncture. Which of the following CSF changes is most likely?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Elevated IgG and myelin basic protein with oligoclonal bands on electrophoresis
Elevated lactate with positive cryptococcal antigen

explanation: MS CSF shows increased IgG, myelin basic protein and oligoclonal bands on electrophoresis.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has numbness and weakness on her left side. Which of the following brain MRI findings best supports multiple sclerosis?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: A longitudinally extensive cord lesion with normal brain imaging
Plaques scattered through the white matter, including along the lateral ventricles

explanation: MS lesions are ovoid T2-hyperintense plaques in the white matter bordering the lateral ventricles and scattered throughout. A longitudinally extensive cord lesion with a normal brain suggests NMO.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has 3 weeks of mild left-sided weakness, increased tone and brisk reflexes. When the pupillary light reflex is tested, her right pupil constricts more when the left eye is illuminated than when the right eye is illuminated. Which of the following best explains the pupillary finding?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: An afferent defect of the right optic nerve (Marcus Gunn pupil)
An efferent defect of the right oculomotor nerve
An efferent defect of the left oculomotor nerve

explanation: A relative afferent defect (Marcus Gunn) of the right optic nerve gives a weaker response from the right eye (direct and consensual) with a normal response from the left. Think MS or optic neuritis.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has double vision on lateral gaze. On looking to either side, the adducting eye does not move past the midline, but convergence is normal. Which structure is demyelinated?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is a lesion of the MLF, with preserved convergence. Bilateral involvement in a young adult is classic for MS.

stem: A 28-year-old woman returns for a 6-month visit. She has new right arm weakness with spasticity. The blurry vision from last year persists, the right-sided sensory loss has improved, and her left-sided weakness has partly recovered. MRI shows periventricular and scattered white matter hyperintensities. Which of the following is the most likely disorder and subtype?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Relapsing episodes with partial recovery, new lesions and periventricular plaques indicate relapsing-remitting MS.

stem: A neurologist explains the difference between multiple sclerosis and Guillain-Barré syndrome to a student. Which of the following correctly pairs each disease with its primary cellular target?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Multiple sclerosis: oligodendrocytes; Guillain-Barré: Schwann cells
Multiple sclerosis: Schwann cells; Guillain-Barré: oligodendrocytes
Multiple sclerosis: neurons; Guillain-Barré: Schwann cells

explanation: MS targets oligodendrocytes (CNS myelin), and Guillain-Barré targets Schwann cells (peripheral myelin). Schwann cells regenerate, so GBS prognosis is better.

stem: A 33-year-old man has progressive leg weakness and tingling. Four weeks ago he had chills and diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken. Reflexes are absent at the knees and ankles. Why is the earlier illness important for this diagnosis?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: The bacteria directly invade the peripheral nerves
A bacterial toxin destroys the anterior horn cells
The organism persists in the CSF
Antibodies and T cells directed at Campylobacter epitopes cross-react with Schwann cell and myelin antigens

explanation: Molecular mimicry: antibodies and T cells against Campylobacter jejuni epitopes cross-react with Schwann cell and myelin antigens.

stem: For the patient in the previous question, nerve conduction studies are ordered. Which of the following is the best choice of region to test first and the expected result?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Arms first; axonal loss with preserved velocities
Legs first (ascending weakness); slowed conduction indicating demyelination
Legs first; absent sensory potentials with normal velocities
Arms first; decremental response on repetitive stimulation

explanation: Weakness ascends, so the legs are tested first. Conduction studies show slowed velocities consistent with demyelination.

stem: A 33-year-old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome is treated with plasma exchange. Which of the following best explains its benefit?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: It replaces the missing myelin proteins
It removes circulating antibodies, complement and cytokines
It kills Campylobacter in the bloodstream

explanation: Plasma exchange removes circulating antibodies, complement and cytokines. IVIG is the alternative and suppresses the autoimmune response. Steroids are not indicated.

stem: On day 5 of hospitalization for Guillain-Barré syndrome, a 40-year-old man has labile blood pressure and episodes of tachycardia. His oxygen saturation and cardiac enzymes are normal. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Dysautonomia, which occurs in about two-thirds of patients

explanation: Dysautonomia occurs in about two-thirds of Guillain-Barré patients and causes labile blood pressure and arrhythmias.

stem: A 10-year-old girl, brought by her adoptive father, has burning leg pain at night, frequent tripping, high-arched feet with hammer toes, and decreased muscle bulk in the legs. Vibration sense is reduced below the ankles, and peroneal motor conduction velocity is reduced. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and cause?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Subacute combined degeneration; vitamin B12 deficiency
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease; autosomal dominant mutation in peripheral myelin protein 22

explanation: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy) is usually an autosomal dominant mutation of PMP22. Findings are pes cavus, hammer toes, distal atrophy and reduced conduction velocity from demyelination.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has optic neuritis in one eye and then transverse myelitis. Which of the following statements best differentiates her disorder from multiple sclerosis?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: It is caused by aquaporin-4 antibodies, typically has more severe symptoms, and preferentially affects the optic nerves and spinal cord
It is caused by antibodies to gangliosides
It is a peripheral demyelinating disease
It is caused by JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes

explanation: NMO is caused by aquaporin-4 antibodies, is typically more severe, and affects the optic nerves and spinal cord. Acute attacks respond to steroids or plasma exchange.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis has a new exacerbation with right leg weakness. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment of the acute exacerbation?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: High-dose corticosteroids treat acute exacerbations. Interferon-β, glatiramer, natalizumab and ocrelizumab are disease-modifying therapies, not acute treatments.

stem: A 55-year-old man has 2 years of progressive spastic weakness of both legs and worsening gait. He has never had a discrete relapse or remission. MRI shows spinal cord and periventricular lesions. Which of the following is the most likely disease course?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Progressive from onset without relapses is primary progressive MS.

stem: A 12-year-old boy with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease has foot drop and distal leg atrophy, with only mild hand weakness. Which of the following best explains why the legs are affected before the arms?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Anterior horn cell loss at L4–S1 only
A length-dependent process affecting the longest peripheral nerves first

explanation: CMT is a length-dependent process, so the longest nerves (to the feet) are involved first.

stem: A 7-year-old boy has a tumor involving the flocculus and nodulus. Which of the following deficits is most likely?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Intention tremor of the arm with dysmetria

explanation: The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) controls the vestibular system. Lesions cause falling, vertigo, nausea and nystagmus.

stem: A patient has a lesion of the nucleus dorsalis (Clarke column) at T10. Which of the following pathways is interrupted?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Clarke nucleus (T1–L2) gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract carrying lower limb unconscious proprioception.

stem: Which of the following describes the second-order neuron for unconscious proprioception from the upper limb?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus in the caudal medulla, giving the cuneocerebellar tract
Nucleus dorsalis of Clarke, giving the dorsal spinocerebellar tract
Nucleus gracilis, giving the medial lemniscus
Ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus

explanation: Upper limb fibers ascend in the fasciculus cuneatus to the accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus in the caudal medulla, which gives the cuneocerebellar tract.

stem: Which of the following cerebellar peduncles carries the output from the dentate nucleus to the thalamus?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle is the main output pathway (dentate to contralateral thalamus). The middle and inferior peduncles are mainly input pathways.

stem: A patient has sudden weakness of the entire right side with a right lower facial droop, hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign. He also has an intention tremor, dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia on the right. MRI shows an infarct in the left crus cerebri. Which of the following best explains the right-sided ataxia?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Interruption of frontopontine fibers of the cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathway in the left crus cerebri

explanation: The crus cerebri carries corticospinal, corticobulbar and frontopontine fibers. Interrupting frontopontine fibers disrupts the cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathway, producing limb ataxia. Fibers of CN III also pass nearby.

stem: A 5-year-old boy with a congenital malformation has absence of the cerebellar vermis. Which of the following is the most likely clinical finding?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Intention tremor of the limbs only
Truncal ataxia with a wide-based gait

explanation: The vermis controls the trunk, so its absence causes truncal ataxia and a wide-based gait (Dandy-Walker malformation).

stem: A patient has a wide-based gait. Which of the following findings best distinguishes sensory ataxia from cerebellar ataxia?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Loss of proprioception, a positive Romberg sign and no vertigo

explanation: Sensory ataxia has loss of proprioception, a positive Romberg sign and no vertigo. Cerebellar ataxia has limb ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus.

stem: A 66-year-old woman has episodic vertigo and rotatory nystagmus when her head is back and her left ear is down. Hearing is normal. Which of the following is the underlying cause?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Displaced otoliths in the semicircular canals

explanation: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is caused by displaced otoliths in the semicircular canals. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver diagnoses it and the Epley maneuver treats it.

stem: A 55-year-old immigrant has sensory ataxia, absent reflexes in the legs and lightning pains. Fluorescent treponemal antibody and CSF-VDRL tests are positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Penicillin and testing of sexual contacts

explanation: Tabes dorsalis is treated with penicillin, and contacts should be tested.

stem: A 15-year-old boy has progressive truncal and limb ataxia, loss of vibration sense and absent ankle reflexes. Which of the following correctly lists the organelle affected and the central nervous system structures involved?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Mitochondria; dorsal columns and spinocerebellar tracts

explanation: Friedreich ataxia (frataxin, GAA repeats in FXN) affects mitochondria and involves the dorsal columns and spinocerebellar tracts.

stem: A patient has a tremor of the left hand only when reaching for a cup. The tremor is absent at rest. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: A tremor that occurs only with movement is an intention (kinetic) tremor, a sign of cerebellar disease. A resting tremor suggests parkinsonism.

stem: A patient with a cerebellar infarct has slurred, indistinct speech. Comprehension, word choice and the amount of speech are normal. Which of the following terms best describes this?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Slurred or indistinct speech with intact comprehension and language use is dysarthria, a mechanical speech disorder. Aphasia is a language disorder.

stem: A 53-year-old man has a new generalized seizure, and a biopsy shows glioblastoma. Which of the following MRI findings is most likely?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: A ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding edema, mass effect, and narrowing of the sulci and ventricles
A cystic lesion with a mural nodule in the cerebellum
A dural-based mass with a dural tail
A lesion in the cerebellopontine angle

explanation: Glioblastoma appears as a ring-enhancing lesion with edema, mass effect, midline shift and narrowing of sulci and ventricles.

stem: A 35-year-old man has new-onset seizures. MRI shows a non-enhancing supratentorial mass. Biopsy shows a hypercellular tumor with nuclear atypia and GFAP positivity, but no necrosis, microvascular proliferation or mitotic activity. Which of the following is the WHO grade?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: An infiltrating (diffuse) astrocytoma with atypia but no necrosis, mitoses or microvascular proliferation is WHO grade II.

stem: A 10-year-old child has cerebellar deficits, and MRI shows a tumor in the cerebellum. Which of the following best describes the most likely tumor?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Ependymoma, WHO grade III, spinal cord
Pilocytic astrocytoma, WHO grade I, ages 8–13, with a biphasic pattern and Rosenthal fibers

explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma: age 8–13, cerebellum, WHO grade I, biphasic, Rosenthal fibers, GFAP positive.

stem: A 2-year-old child has had a month of constant crying and head-pointing, then daily vomiting and a wobbly gait. He has bilateral papilledema and a wide-based gait, but normal finger-to-nose testing. Which of the following structures best explains his findings?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: The cerebellar vermis or nodulus, with compression of the fourth ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus

explanation: Truncal ataxia without limb ataxia points to the vermis or nodulus. Compression of the fourth ventricle causes obstructive hydrocephalus. This is medulloblastoma.

stem: Why should a lumbar puncture be avoided in the child in the previous question?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: With raised intracranial pressure and papilledema, withdrawal of lumbar CSF can cause herniation of the brain through the foramen magnum

explanation: Papilledema indicates raised intracranial pressure. Lumbar puncture can cause herniation through the foramen magnum.

stem: A 9-year-old boy has 2 months of headache and lethargy. T2 MRI shows a mass in the left lateral ventricle, with enlargement of the ventricle and shift of the septum pellucidum. Which of the following histologic features is most likely?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Ependymomas have perivascular pseudorosettes and ependymal rosettes.

stem: A 60-year-old woman has 2 months of headache, social withdrawal and impaired recall. MRI shows a large right frontal mass with a dural tail, and resection shows cellular whorls and psammoma bodies. Which of the following best explains why symptoms began only 2 months ago?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: The tumor grows slowly and the brain accommodates displacement until the mass is large
The tumor invades the brain rapidly
The tumor obstructs CSF flow early

explanation: Meningiomas are slow-growing, and the brain accommodates displacement until the tumor is large.

stem: A 38-year-old man has seizures. Which of the following correctly describes oligodendroglioma?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Cerebellar tumor of children, WHO grade I
Supratentorial tumor of adults aged 35–44 years, WHO grade II, with a chicken-wire capillary pattern
Tumor of the cerebellopontine angle with Antoni A areas

explanation: Oligodendroglioma: ages 35–44, supratentorial, WHO grade II, fried-egg cells and chicken-wire capillaries.

stem: A 6-year-old child has temporal lobe seizures. Resection of a hemispheric grade I tumor shows binucleated ganglion cells with peripheral Nissl substance, glial cells and calcifications. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Ganglioglioma is a grade I hemispheric tumor of children presenting with seizures, with binucleated ganglion cells, glia and calcifications.

stem: A surgeon explains why a schwannoma can be removed while sparing the nerve, but a neurofibroma usually cannot. Which of the following best explains this?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Schwannomas always occur in the brain
Schwannomas displace adjacent nerve fibers, while neurofibromas infiltrate through the nerve

explanation: Schwannomas displace nerve fibers and can be shelled out. Neurofibromas infiltrate the nerve and cannot be removed without sacrificing it.

stem: Neurofibromatosis type 2 is caused by defects in the gene encoding merlin. Which of the following best describes how this leads to schwannomas?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Merlin normally suppresses cell growth in crowded environments, so its loss allows uninhibited Schwann cell growth
Merlin inhibits mTOR, so its loss increases cell size
Merlin is a Ras GTPase-activating protein

explanation: Merlin is a cell adhesion molecule that suppresses growth in crowded cell environments, so its loss allows uninhibited Schwann cell growth.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, a feeling of ear fullness and nausea. MRI shows a tumor at the cerebellopontine angle along cranial nerve VIII. Which of the following best describes the symptoms of this tumor?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness and nausea from a vestibular schwannoma

explanation: Vestibular schwannoma (CN VIII, cerebellopontine angle) causes vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness and nausea.

stem: A clinician diagnoses neurofibromatosis type 1 when at least two criteria are met. Which of the following single findings counts as one criterion?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Two or more neurofibromas of any type, or one plexiform neurofibroma

explanation: Two or more neurofibromas of any type, or one plexiform neurofibroma, is a criterion. Diagnosis requires two or more criteria.

stem: A 12-year-old with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a tortuous mass along a nerve that feels like a bag of worms. Which of the following is true about this lesion?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: It is a plexiform neurofibroma, virtually pathognomonic for NF1

explanation: A plexiform neurofibroma (“bag of worms”) is virtually pathognomonic for NF1.

stem: A child with neurofibromatosis type 1 has pigmented nodules on the iris. Which of the following describes Lisch nodules?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Lisch nodules are melanocytic hamartomas of the iris seen in NF1.

stem: A 22-year-old has bilateral vestibular schwannomas and cataracts. Which of the following is the most likely disorder, and which chromosome carries the gene?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas and cataracts indicate NF2 (merlin, chromosome 22). NF1 is chromosome 17 (neurofibromin).

stem: A 20-year-old woman with bilateral flank pain and hematuria has facial angiofibromas, a leathery back patch, periungual fibromas and bilateral renal angiomyolipomas. She has had epilepsy since childhood. Which of the following correctly describes the genes involved?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: TSC1 and TSC2, tumor suppressors encoding hamartin and tuberin that normally inhibit mTOR
NF1, encoding a Ras GTPase-activating protein
VHL, encoding a protein that degrades HIF

explanation: Tuberous sclerosis: TSC1 (chromosome 9, hamartin) and TSC2 (chromosome 16, tuberin), whose complex inhibits mTOR.

stem: MRI in a patient with tuberous sclerosis shows periventricular calcified nodules that resemble candle gutterings. One of these enlarges and obstructs the foramen of Monro. Which of the following is the most likely tumor?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Subependymal nodules (“candle gutterings”) can enlarge into a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma.

stem: Which of the following best defines a cortical tuber in tuberous sclerosis?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: A calcified tumor of the choroid plexus
An enlarged gyrus with disorganized lamination and no clear separation of gray and white matter
A cystic lesion with a mural nodule
A cluster of whorled arachnoid cells
A heterotopic nodule of normal neurons

explanation: A tuber is an enlarged gyrus with disorganized neurons and glia, lacking separation of gray and white matter.

stem: An infant with a port-wine stain and seizures is diagnosed with Sturge-Weber syndrome. Which of the following best describes the histology and genetics?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Leptomeningeal (arachnoid-pia) angiomas with cortical calcification; somatic GNAQ mutation on chromosome 9

explanation: Sturge-Weber: leptomeningeal angiomas, cortical calcification (tram-track), somatic GNAQ mutation on chromosome 9.

stem: A 28-year-old man with von Hippel-Lindau disease has a cerebellar hemangioblastoma. Which of the following best describes this tumor and the gene?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Composed of whorled meningothelial cells; NF2
Composed of astrocytes with Rosenthal fibers; NF1
Composed of endothelial cells, pericytes and stromal cells; VHL gene on chromosome 3p25.3

explanation: VHL hemangioblastomas are made of endothelial cells, pericytes and stromal cells. The gene is on chromosome 3p25.3.

stem: A 45-year-old man has fever, headache and confusion. Brain biopsy shows a viral encephalitis. Which of the following pathologic changes is typical?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates, neuronophagia and microglial nodules

explanation: Viral encephalitis shows perivascular lymphocytic infiltration, neuronophagia, microglial nodules and vasogenic edema.

stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV has a slowly progressive, painless gait disturbance with neurogenic bladder and spastic paraparesis. Examination shows dorsal column dysfunction, and MRI of the thoracic cord shows no compression. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: HIV vacuolar myelopathy affects the thoracic cord and causes slowly progressive painless gait disturbance, neurogenic bladder, spastic paraparesis and dorsal column dysfunction. Syphilis, TB, HTLV-1 and B12 deficiency are in the differential.

stem: A 50-year-old man who owns a cat hotel has HIV, headache, low-grade fever and slowed thinking. MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Which of the following is the most likely route of acquisition of the responsible organism?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Oocysts from cat feces or cysts in undercooked meat, followed by reactivation

explanation: Toxoplasma gondii is acquired from cat feces oocysts or undercooked meat, and reactivates at CD4 below 100/µL.

stem: A 35-year-old man with AIDS and CD4 count 40/µL has meningoencephalitis. Which of the following is the most likely set of findings?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Marked neutrophilic pleocytosis and gram-positive diplococci
Mildly elevated opening pressure in most patients, mild mononuclear pleocytosis, India ink positivity, and no contrast enhancement on MRI

explanation: Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis: raised opening pressure in about 70%, mild mononuclear pleocytosis, India ink and antigen positivity, and no enhancement on MRI.

stem: A 51-year-old woman with aggressive multiple sclerosis is placed on immunosuppression. Two years later she develops bilateral blindness, cognitive decline and unsteadiness. CSF is positive for JC virus DNA. MRI shows demyelination extending through the posterior parietal and occipital lobes of both hemispheres. Which of the following best explains her blindness?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Bilateral demyelination of the optic radiations

explanation: Demyelination extending through the posterior parietal and occipital white matter damages the optic radiations bilaterally, causing bilateral blindness. PML occurs with any immunosuppression.

stem: Which of the following findings best favors primary CNS lymphoma over toxoplasmosis in a patient with AIDS?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Multiple lesions in the basal ganglia
CD4 below 50/µL, a solitary lesion, EBV association, and elevated CSF protein, LDH and β2-microglobulin

explanation: PCNSL: CD4 below 50/µL, solitary lesion, EBV, and elevated CSF protein, LDH and β2-microglobulin.

stem: A 40-year-old man with AIDS (CD4 count 30/µL) has retinitis, rapidly progressive dementia and multiple cranial neuropathies. MRI shows periventricular enhancement. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: CMV (CD4 below 50/µL) causes retinitis, ventriculoencephalitis with rapidly progressive dementia and cranial neuropathies, and polyradiculitis.

stem: A patient with HIV and tuberculous meningitis improves, then worsens clinically after antiretroviral therapy is started, with fever and neurologic deterioration. CD4 count has risen. Which of the following is the most appropriate description of this syndrome?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, an exaggerated inflammatory response to a previously acquired infection

explanation: IRIS follows immune recovery and is an exaggerated inflammatory response to a previously acquired infection (Cryptococcus, TB, MAC). Severe cases are treated with steroids.

stem: A 63-year-old man with fever and confusion has CSF PCR positive for HSV-1. Which of the following describes the likely route of CNS entry?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Spread through the cribriform plate from the sinuses
Migration along the trigeminal or olfactory nerve to the temporal and frontal lobes

explanation: HSV-1 enters the CNS by migrating along the trigeminal or olfactory nerve.

stem: Brain biopsy of the patient in the previous question is most likely to show which of the following?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates with Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions

explanation: HSV encephalitis shows perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and Cowdry type A inclusion bodies in neurons and glia, with a hemorrhagic temporal lesion.

stem: A 60-year-old man has a painful vesicular rash along a band on the left side of his chest. Which of the following best explains the rash?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Spread of herpes simplex from the lip
Reactivation of varicella zoster virus dormant in a dorsal root ganglion, traveling along the sensory nerve

explanation: VZV remains dormant in dorsal root ganglia and reactivates, traveling along the sensory nerve to cause a dermatomal vesicular rash.

stem: A 10-year-old girl was bitten by a raccoon and died 2 months later after developing agitation and hydrophobia. Which of the following would be seen in her neurons?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Rabies causes Negri bodies in neurons. The virus travels along peripheral nerves to the CNS.

stem: A 55-year-old man with fever, headache and acute flaccid paralysis of one limb has west Nile virus infection. Which of the following best explains the paralysis?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Lower motor neuron injury of the anterior horn of the spinal cord

explanation: West Nile virus injures anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons), causing flaccid paralysis.

stem: A 15-year-old boy develops a rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis after swimming in a freshwater lake. CSF shows motile amoebae. Which of the following is the most likely organism?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Naegleria fowleri causes rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis after freshwater exposure, with amoebae in the CSF.

stem: A newborn has meningitis. Which of the following characteristics identifies Listeria monocytogenes in culture?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: A thick polysaccharide capsule on India ink

explanation: Listeria shows tumbling motility in culture and affects neonates, the elderly and immunocompromised patients.

stem: A man has sudden weakness and sensory loss of the left leg and foot only. Which of the following best explains why the leg area is supplied differently from the arm and face areas?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: The leg area lies on the lateral hemisphere supplied by the middle cerebral artery
The leg area lies in the paracentral lobule on the medial surface, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, while the arm and face areas lie laterally and are supplied by the middle cerebral artery
The leg area is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery
The leg area is supplied by the vertebral artery
The leg area is supplied by the lenticulostriate arteries

explanation: The leg and foot area lies in the paracentral lobule on the medial surface (ACA). The arm, trunk and face areas lie on the lateral surface (MCA).

stem: Which of the following sets of structures is supplied by the anterior choroidal artery?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Primary motor cortex and Broca area
Medial frontal lobe and corpus callosum
Hippocampus, amygdala, Meyer loop, choroid plexus and the inferior portion of the posterior limb of the internal capsule

explanation: The anterior choroidal artery supplies the hippocampus, amygdala, Meyer loop, choroid plexus, LGN and the inferior posterior limb of the internal capsule.

stem: On a lateral-view cerebral angiogram, which of the following helps identify the anterior cerebral artery?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: It runs through the sylvian fissure
It ascends over the convexity laterally
It arises from the vertebral artery
It curves around the corpus callosum

explanation: On the lateral view, the ACA is identified by its curve around the corpus callosum.

stem: A patient with a 20-year history of diabetes has sudden painless loss of vision in the right eye. There is no direct or consensual pconstriction when light is shone in the right eye, and the left eye responds normally. Which of the following vessels gives rise to the artery involved?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: The ophthalmic artery is a branch of the ICA. Occlusion (retinal artery) causes monocular blindness with an afferent pupillary defect (no direct or consensual response from the affected eye).

stem: A woman keeps bumping her head on kitchen cabinet doors. Examination shows a right upper homonymous quadrantanopia. Which of the following structures is most likely damaged?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Left Meyer loop in the temporal lobe

explanation: A right upper homonymous quadrantanopia (“pie in the sky”) is a left temporal Meyer loop lesion (MCA or PCA territory). Parietal radiations carry the inferior field.

stem: A man suddenly loses sensation over the right neck, upper limb and abdomen. His speech is fluent but contains fabricated words, and he cannot follow verbal commands. Which of the following is the most likely lesion and vessel?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Left anterior cerebral artery; paracentral lobule
Left middle cerebral artery (inferior division); superior posterior temporal lobe
Left posterior cerebral artery; occipital lobe
Right middle cerebral artery; posterior parietal lobe

explanation: Wernicke aphasia and right sensory loss: inferior division of the left MCA affecting the superior posterior temporal lobe and adjacent parietal cortex.

stem: A woman has sudden right upper limb weakness with hyperreflexia and increased tone. She tries to answer questions but produces no words, yet follows verbal commands. Which of the following is the most likely lesion and vessel?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Left Wernicke area; inferior division of the MCA
Left posterior inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area); MCA

explanation: Right arm weakness with no speech but intact comprehension is Broca aphasia: the posterior inferior frontal gyrus, MCA.

stem: A patient after a stroke has nonfluent speech, intact comprehension and intact repetition. Which of the following is the most likely location?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Medial frontal lobe near Broca area, in the ACA/MCA watershed

explanation: Transcortical motor aphasia (nonfluent, comprehension and repetition intact) involves the medial frontal lobe near Broca area, in the ACA/MCA watershed.

stem: A patient after a stroke has fluent speech with impaired comprehension but intact repetition. Which of the following is the most likely location?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: A region adjacent to Wernicke area in the MCA/PCA watershed

explanation: Transcortical sensory aphasia (fluent, impaired comprehension, intact repetition) involves cortex adjacent to Wernicke area, in the MCA/PCA watershed.

stem: A patient after a large perisylvian infarct cannot name objects, speak fluently, comprehend, repeat or read. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Global aphasia, from extensive left MCA territory infarction involving Broca area, Wernicke area and the arcuate fasciculus

explanation: Global aphasia (nonfluent, poor comprehension and repetition) results from an extensive MCA infarct involving Broca area, Wernicke area and the arcuate fasciculus.

stem: A student confuses aphasia with dysarthria. Which of the following statements is correct?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Both are disorders of muscle coordination
Aphasia is a cognitive language disorder affecting spoken, written and sign language, while dysarthria is a mechanical disorder of the muscles of speech
Aphasia is caused only by cerebellar lesions

explanation: Aphasia is a cognitive language disorder across spoken, written and sign language. Dysarthria is a mechanical disorder of the muscles of speech, including from cerebellar lesions.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches the brainstem level with its blood supply?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Midbrain: basilar artery only; pons: PCA; medulla: AICA
Midbrain: PICA; pons: ASA; medulla: SCA
Midbrain: AICA; pons: PICA; medulla: PCA
Midbrain: PCA; rostral pons: SCA and basilar; caudal pons: AICA; medulla: PICA, vertebral and anterior spinal arteries

explanation: Midbrain: PCA. Rostral pons: SCA (long circumferential) and basilar. Caudal pons: AICA. Medulla: PICA, vertebral and anterior spinal arteries.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes venous drainage of the brain?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Superficial veins drain to the superior sagittal sinus, deep veins drain to the straight sinus through the great cerebral vein, and the sinuses empty into the internal jugular vein
Deep veins drain directly to the internal carotid artery
Superficial veins drain to the straight sinus
Dural sinuses drain to the vertebral veins only
The sagittal sinus drains into the cavernous sinus

explanation: Superficial veins drain to the superior sagittal sinus, deep veins drain to the straight sinus (great cerebral vein of Galen), and the sinuses empty into the internal jugular vein.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes berry aneurysms and the sites prone to hypertensive hemorrhage?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Berry aneurysms occur in the cerebellum; hypertensive bleeds occur in the cortex
Berry aneurysms occur at vein junctions; hypertensive bleeds occur at the pituitary
Berry aneurysms occur in the spinal cord
Berry aneurysms occur in the optic nerve; hypertensive bleeds occur in the hippocampus
Berry aneurysms occur at branch points around the circle of Willis; hypertensive bleeds occur in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons and cerebellum

explanation: Berry aneurysms form at branch points around the circle of Willis. Hypertension damages long, narrow vessels, causing hemorrhages in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons and cerebellum.

stem: A 56-year-old man has two 10-minute episodes of right facial numbness that fully resolved. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: It is benign and needs only routine follow-up
It has no risk of stroke
It is a medical emergency, with about 5% risk of stroke within 2 days and about 11% within 90 days
It always causes a visible infarct on CT
It occurs only in the elderly

explanation: A TIA is a medical emergency. About 5% have a stroke within 2 days and about 11% within 90 days.

stem: Which of the following best describes the sequence of events in atherosclerotic plaque formation?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Smooth muscle death, then fat loss
Fat deposition in the intima, macrophage cytokine release causing inflammation, smooth muscle proliferation and connective tissue deposition, and plaque growth

explanation: Plaque formation: fat in the intima, macrophage cytokines causing inflammation, smooth muscle proliferation and connective tissue deposition, and plaque growth.

stem: A 75-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has a lacunar infarct. Which of the following correctly pairs the pathologic process with the vessels affected and risk factors?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Lipohyalinosis; lenticulostriate, thalamic perforator and basilar branch vessels; hypertension, diabetes and aging
Embolism; middle cerebral artery; atrial fibrillation

explanation: Lipohyalinosis (endothelial damage and wall thickening) affects lenticulostriate, thalamic perforator and basilar branch vessels. Risks are hypertension, diabetes and aging.

stem: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has a cortical infarct. Which of the following are the most common sources of embolic stroke?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: The heart and the internal carotid artery

explanation: Emboli come most commonly from the heart (atrial fibrillation) and the internal carotid artery. Treatment is anticoagulation and control of atrial fibrillation.

stem: A 41-year-old woman develops a stroke 2 weeks after a neck procedure. Which of the following correctly describes arterial dissection?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Separation of the intima and media with an expanding intramural hematoma

explanation: Arterial dissection is a separation of the intima and media with an expanding intramural hematoma, associated with trauma and hypertension.

stem: A patient has headache, stiff neck and nausea. Which of the following findings best distinguishes subarachnoid hemorrhage from meningitis?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Fever and neutrophils in the CSF
No fever, red blood cells in the CSF, and blood in the sulcal spaces on CT

explanation: SAH is afebrile, with red blood cells in the CSF and blood in the subarachnoid space on CT. Meningitis has fever and meningeal inflammation.

stem: A 59-year-old man has a ruptured saccular aneurysm of the anterior cerebral artery. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment of the aneurysm?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Clipping or coiling, with blood pressure control

explanation: Aneurysms are treated by clipping or coiling, with blood pressure control. Complications are vasospasm (nimodipine) and hydrocephalus.

stem: A neurology student reviews cerebral blood flow. Which of the following statements is correct?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Blood flow is highly sensitive to oxygen levels
Blood flow decreases with high CO2
Blood flow changes linearly with blood pressure
Blood flow is constant over a restricted range of arterial pressure, insensitive to oxygen, and very sensitive to CO2 (high CO2 lowers pH and causes vasodilation)
Blood flow is unaffected by CO2

explanation: Cerebral blood flow is constant over a range of pressures, insensitive to oxygen and very sensitive to CO2.

stem: A patient is brought in by EMS with symptoms of stroke. Which of the following correctly lists the initial imaging sequence?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Noncontrast CT to distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke, then CT angiography to find the occlusion, then CT perfusion to assess viable tissue

explanation: Noncontrast CT separates ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke, CTA locates the occlusion, and CT perfusion shows viable tissue. Then decide on thrombolysis or thrombectomy.

stem: A researcher asks which brain regions have neurons most sensitive to ischemia. Which of the following is correct?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: The hippocampus, cerebellum and cortex have neurons most sensitive to ischemia.

stem: A 42-year-old man with a prior right MCA stroke, tobacco and cannabis use, LDL 65 mg/dL and HbA1c 8.9% returns with new vision loss. Workup finds intracranial atherosclerosis. Which of the following is the most important management priority?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Aggressive control of vascular risk factors: glycemic control, antiplatelet therapy, statin, and cessation of smoking and drug use

explanation: Recurrent stroke from intracranial atherosclerosis with poorly controlled risk factors requires aggressive control of glucose, antiplatelet therapy, statin, and cessation of smoking and drug use.

stem: A 20-year-old man is in a coma after head trauma. Which of the following correctly lists the requirements for a diagnosis of brain death?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Lack of brain function, lack of cranial nerve function and loss of all brainstem reflexes

explanation: Brain death requires lack of brain function, lack of cranial nerve function and loss of all brainstem reflexes.

stem: In the patient in the previous question, infusion of cold water into each ear produces no eye movement. Which of the following brainstem levels does this test assess, and what does the result suggest?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Rostral medulla to caudal pons (vestibulo-ocular pathway); likely irreversible bilateral brainstem damage at this level

explanation: The caloric test assesses the vestibulo-ocular pathway from the rostral medulla to the caudal pons. Absence suggests irreversible brainstem damage at that level.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches brainstem level to the reflex used to assess it?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Midbrain: gag; pons: pupillary; medulla: corneal
Midbrain: corneal; pons: gag; medulla: pupillary
Midbrain: oculocephalic; pons: gag; medulla: corneal
Midbrain: caloric; pons: cough; medulla: pupillary
Midbrain: pupillary light reflex; pons: corneal reflex; medulla: oculocephalic reflex

explanation: Midbrain: pupillary light reflex. Pons: corneal reflex. Medulla: oculocephalic (vestibulo-ocular) reflex or caloric test.

stem: A 16-year-old with a facial furuncle has cavernous sinus thrombosis. Which of the following cranial nerves lie within the cavernous sinus?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: III, IV, V1, V2 and VI

explanation: The cavernous sinus contains the ICA, CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI, and sympathetic fibers.

stem: A patient has a sudden stroke. Which of the following findings favors a cortical rather than a subcortical location?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Pure motor hemiparesis of face, arm and leg
Pure sensory loss of face and body
Aphasia, sustained eye deviation or a visual field cut without cranial nerve palsies
Cranial nerve palsies with crossed findings

explanation: Cortical strokes cause aphasia, sustained eye deviation, visual field cuts, cognitive deficits and face/arm without leg (or leg alone) deficits, without cranial nerve palsies other than lower face.

stem: A patient has right lower facial droop with forehead sparing and no other cranial nerve findings. Which of the following is the best interpretation?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: An upper motor neuron lesion of the left corticobulbar pathway

explanation: Lower facial weakness with forehead sparing is an upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesion on the opposite side. A CN VII lesion paralyzes the whole face on the same side.

stem: Which of the following best differentiates a proximal from a distal middle cerebral artery infarct?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Distal infarcts cause hemiparesis of the entire contralateral body
Proximal infarcts involve the lenticulostriate branches and internal capsule, causing weakness of the entire contralateral body, while distal infarcts affect the face and arm sparing the leg
Distal infarcts cause leg weakness only

explanation: Proximal MCA infarcts involve lenticulostriate branches and the internal capsule (whole contralateral body). Distal infarcts affect the face and arm and spare the leg.

stem: A patient has an infarct of the right frontal eye field. Which of the following is the most likely eye finding?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Each frontal eye field drives gaze to the opposite side, so a right infarct causes sustained gaze to the right (toward the lesion).

stem: An 80-year-old woman ignores her left side, draws all the clock numbers on the right and is unaware of the problem. Which of the following is the most likely lesion and vessel?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Neglect and anosognosia: right posterior parietal lobe, MCA.

stem: A patient has right arm and leg weakness with hyperreflexia, a Babinski sign, right mouth droop with forehead sparing and tongue deviation to the right. His left eye is down and out, with a dilated pupil, no direct or consensual response and inability to look up or down. Sensation is intact. Which of the following is the most likely lesion and vessel?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Left rostral midbrain; posterior cerebral artery

explanation: Weber syndrome: left rostral midbrain (CN III ipsilateral, corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers contralateral), PCA. The tongue deviation is from corticobulbar (UMN) involvement, not CN XII.

stem: A 76-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped warfarin. She now has a right eye down and out with a dilated pupil, loss of touch on the left body, loss of touch and pinprick on the left face, and left limb intention tremor. Which of the following sets of structures is involved?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Right CN III, medial lemniscus, ventral trigeminothalamic tract and superior cerebellar peduncle in the right midbrain
Left CN III, corticospinal tract and medial lemniscus
Right CN VI and facial nucleus
Left CN V and spinal trigeminal tract

explanation: Benedikt syndrome: right CN III, medial lemniscus, ventral trigeminothalamic tract and superior cerebellar peduncle fibers in the right midbrain, from PCA.

stem: A 66-year-old man has double vision with the right eye down and out and a dilated pupil, left limb ataxia, and mild slowness and stiffness of the left arm. Strength and sensation are normal, and the face and tongue are symmetric. Which of the following structures best explain the left-sided findings?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Right superior cerebellar peduncle and substantia nigra

explanation: The right superior cerebellar peduncle (after decussation) and substantia nigra explain the left ataxia and parkinsonian stiffness. The red nucleus alone supplies only the upper limb.

stem: A patient has sudden jaw deviation to the right, loss of touch on the right face, and right arm and leg dysmetria with tremor. Strength and sensation elsewhere are intact. Which of the following is the most likely lesion?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Right mid pons, including trigeminal motor nucleus, chief sensory nucleus and cerebellar peduncle fibers

explanation: CN V marks the mid pons. Jaw deviation, ipsilateral facial touch loss and ipsilateral ataxia (peduncle fibers) localize to the right mid pons (basilar).

stem: A 59-year-old woman has sudden facial numbness and trouble chewing. Her jaw deviates to the right. She has loss of light touch on the right face, loss of pain and temperature on the left body, and right ptosis and miosis with decreased facial sweating. Coordination is normal. Which of the following explains the findings?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Right mid pons: motor and chief sensory nuclei of V, anterolateral system and sympathetic fibers, with sparing of the cerebellar peduncles

explanation: The same mid pontine lesion without ataxia: motor and chief sensory nuclei of V, anterolateral system and sympathetic fibers, with the cerebellar peduncles spared.

stem: A 61-year-old man has horizontal diplopia, with the left eye turned medially and unable to abduct. He has right arm and leg weakness, right lower face droop with forehead sparing, and loss of right-sided touch. Which of the following is the most likely location?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Left medial caudal pons (abducens, corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, medial lemniscus)

explanation: CN VI with contralateral weakness and a UMN lower face droop is an alternating syndrome of the left medial caudal pons (basilar paramedian branches).

stem: A 55-year-old woman has complete right facial paralysis including the forehead, loss of pain and temperature on the right face and left body, and right ptosis and miosis. Coordination and strength are normal. Which of the following is the most likely lesion and vessel?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Right lateral caudal pons; anterior inferior cerebellar artery
Right medial pons; basilar paramedian branches

explanation: Whole-face palsy, ipsilateral face and contralateral body pain and temperature loss, and Horner syndrome localize to the right lateral caudal pons (AICA). Coordination is normal because the peduncles are spared.

stem: A 57-year-old man with hypertension suddenly has vertigo, vomiting and hoarseness. He has nystagmus, truncal ataxia and left limb ataxia, and the uvula deviates to the right. He has loss of pain and temperature in the left face and right body, with small left pupil and ptosis. Which of the following structures explains the left limb ataxia, and which vessel is involved?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Wallenberg syndrome: left inferior cerebellar peduncle damage causes left limb ataxia (PICA or vertebral artery).

stem: A 63-year-old man has weakness of the left arm and leg with hyperreflexia, tongue deviation to the right, and loss of vibration and proprioception in the left limbs. Pinprick is intact and the face moves normally. Which of the following is the most likely lesion and vessel?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Right rostral medulla (medial), involving corticospinal tract, hypoglossal nerve and medial lemniscus; anterior spinal artery

explanation: Right medial rostral medulla: right corticospinal tract (left weakness), right CN XII (tongue to the right) and right medial lemniscus (left vibration and proprioception loss). Supply is the anterior spinal artery.

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is awake and alert, quadriplegic, unable to speak or swallow, and can communicate only by blinking and moving his eyes vertically. Which of the following is the most likely lesion and vessel?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Bilateral basal pons (corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts); basilar artery

explanation: Locked-in syndrome results from bilateral basal pontine infarction of the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts (basilar artery), sparing consciousness and vertical gaze.

stem: A 72-year-old man has right arm, leg and lower face weakness with hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign. He has no sensory loss, cranial nerve palsy other than lower face, ataxia, or cognitive or visual deficits. Which of the following is the most likely location, and why is this not a brainstem lesion?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Right thalamus; because sensory loss would be present
Left medial medulla; because the tongue would be affected
Left posterior limb of the internal capsule (lenticulostriate lacune); because brainstem lesions produce crossed cranial nerve findings
Left cerebellum; because ataxia would be present
Left occipital lobe; because vision would be affected

explanation: Pure motor hemiparesis of the face, arm and leg without crossed or cranial nerve findings is a lacunar infarct of the posterior limb of the internal capsule (lenticulostriate arteries).

stem: An 82-year-old woman with a urinary tract infection develops confusion over 2 days. She is inattentive, her alertness fluctuates, and her speech is disorganized. Which of the following best describes her condition compared with dementia?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Abrupt onset, reduced attention, fluctuating consciousness, usually reversible
Chronic course lasting years with stable consciousness

explanation: Delirium: abrupt onset, reduced attention, fluctuating consciousness, disorganized speech, usually reversible. Dementia: insidious, normal attention, irreversible.

stem: Patient H.M. had bilateral medial temporal lobe resection. Which of the following is the most accurate prediction after surgery?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: He can learn to ride a bicycle (procedural memory intact), but he will not remember having learned it
He loses all memory types equally

explanation: H.M. lost new episodic and semantic memory but kept procedural and working memory. He could learn a bicycle but not remember learning it.

stem: A man has bilateral amygdala damage after herpes encephalitis. Which of the following findings is most likely?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Loss of fear and aggression, hypo-emotionality, hyperorality and hypersexuality (Klüver-Bucy syndrome)

explanation: Bilateral amygdala damage causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome: loss of fear and aggression, hypo-emotionality, hyperorality and hypersexuality.

stem: A researcher studies the nucleus accumbens. Which of the following best describes its role?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Mediates response to rewarding stimuli through dopamine, reinforcing rewarding behaviors and contributing to addiction

explanation: The nucleus accumbens mediates reward through dopamine and reinforces rewarding behaviors, which is central to addiction.

stem: Which of the following correctly lists the progression of activity through the Papez circuit?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Hippocampus, fornix, mammillary body, anterior thalamic nucleus, cingulate gyrus, entorhinal cortex, hippocampus

explanation: Papez circuit: hippocampus, fornix, mammillary body, anterior thalamic nucleus, cingulate gyrus, entorhinal cortex, back to the hippocampus.

stem: A 50-year-old man who drinks two pints of vodka daily is confused, with bilateral horizontal nystagmus and an unsteady, wide-based gait. Which of the following correctly states the classic triad and the MRI finding?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia; hemorrhage of the mammillary bodies

explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency): confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia. MRI shows hemorrhage of the mammillary bodies. Give IV thiamine before glucose. Untreated, Korsakoff syndrome (anterograde amnesia, confabulation) can follow.

stem: Which of the following best describes how amyloid and tau are involved in Alzheimer disease?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Amyloid forms intracellular tangles and tau forms extracellular plaques
Both aggregate only in the cerebellum

Improper cleavage of amyloid precursor protein by secretases produces long β-amyloid fragments that aggregate into extracellular plaques, and hyperphosphorylated tau forms intracellular neurofibrillary tangles

explanation: Improper cleavage of APP by secretases yields long β-amyloid fragments that form extracellular plaques, while hyperphosphorylated tau forms intracellular tangles.

stem: MRI of a patient with Alzheimer disease shows cortical atrophy with enlarged lateral ventricles. Which of the following explains the ventricular enlargement, and which cholinergic structure degenerates?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Hydrocephalus ex vacuo from loss of cortical tissue; nucleus basalis of Meynert

explanation: Cortical atrophy causes hydrocephalus ex vacuo. Cholinergic loss follows degeneration of the nucleus basalis of Meynert, which is why cholinesterase inhibitors are used.

stem: A 64-year-old man has REM sleep behavior disorder, visual hallucinations and fluctuating cognition. Which of the following would be found at autopsy?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Lewy bodies containing α-synuclein, diffusely in the cortex and in the substantia nigra
Pick bodies in the frontal lobe

explanation: Lewy body dementia: Lewy bodies of α-synuclein (with neuromelanin) in the cortex and substantia nigra. Memory is spared early.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes frontotemporal lobar degeneration subtypes?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Memory loss first and hippocampal atrophy
Behavioral variant from frontal lobe damage, and primary progressive aphasia from Broca area (speech) or Wernicke area (comprehension) involvement, with tau or TDP-43 inclusions

explanation: Behavioral variant arises from frontal damage. Primary progressive aphasia arises from Broca area (speech) or Wernicke area (comprehension) involvement. Pathology is tau or TDP-43.

stem: A 63-year-old woman has rapidly progressive confusion, ataxia and myoclonus. Which of the following sets of findings is most likely?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Hippocampal atrophy on MRI; neuritic plaques
MRI cortical ribboning with caudate, putamen and thalamic hyperintensity; periodic sharp waves on EEG; 14-3-3 in the CSF

explanation: CJD: rapid decline, myoclonus and ataxia, with cortical ribboning and basal ganglia and thalamic hyperintensity, periodic sharp waves on EEG and 14-3-3 in CSF.

stem: A 72-year-old man has a magnetic gait, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline, with enlarged ventricles. Which of the following is the best description of the disorder and its treatment?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Normal pressure hydrocephalus from impaired CSF resorption by the arachnoid granulations; shunting

explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus: gait disorder, dementia and urinary incontinence from impaired CSF resorption by arachnoid granulations. Treat with shunting.

stem: Which of the following best differentiates vascular dementia from Alzheimer disease?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Stepwise progression with focal neurologic deficits from multiple infarcts
Insidious memory loss as the first feature

explanation: Vascular dementia has stepwise progression and focal deficits from multiple infarcts. Memory impairment tends to occur later. AD has insidious memory loss.

stem: According to your course notes, which MMSE score range indicates mild cognitive impairment?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Per your course notes, an MMSE of 26–21 indicates mild cognitive impairment.

stem: A 42-year-old man has chorea, depression and dementia. His father had similar symptoms. Which of the following correctly describes this disease?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Autosomal dominant CAG repeats in the huntingtin gene, with caudate and putamen atrophy, dopamine excess relative to acetylcholine, and tetrabenazine treatment

explanation: Huntington disease: autosomal dominant CAG repeats in huntingtin, caudate and putamen atrophy, dopamine excess relative to acetylcholine, treated with tetrabenazine.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has a strange sensation followed by involuntary contraction of her right arm. She remains fully aware and can answer questions throughout. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Focal aware seizure: focal symptoms with preserved awareness.

stem: A 28-year-old man has a warning sensation, then stares, picks at his clothes and smacks his lips, and does not respond. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Focal impaired awareness seizure with automatisms

explanation: Focal impaired awareness seizure: aura plus impaired awareness with automatisms.

stem: A 20-year-old woman in class suddenly stiffens for about 20 seconds, then is sleepy and confused. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Tonic seizure: stiffening of the body, then postictal drowsiness and confusion.

stem: A 35-year-old man at work cries out, falls stiff, and then has rhythmic jerking of all limbs for about 1 minute. He is incontinent and sleepy afterward. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Tonic-clonic seizure: alternating stiffening and jerking, incontinence and postictal confusion.

stem: A 10-year-old girl has sudden, brief, shock-like jerks of both shoulders and arms for about 4 seconds, with several episodes a day. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Myoclonic seizure: brief repetitive jerks of the arms or legs.

stem: A 30-year-old woman who was talking suddenly falls to the ground motionless. She does not respond and is confused afterward. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Atonic (drop) seizure: sudden loss of tone and falling.

stem: A 6-year-old boy does not respond when called on in class. He stares to the side, blinks several times for about 20 seconds, and then resumes talking. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Absence seizure: blank stare with blinking, no postictal period.

stem: A student asks how focal and generalized seizures differ. Which of the following is correct?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Focal seizures always cause loss of consciousness
Focal seizures begin in one area of one hemisphere and can spread (secondary generalization), while generalized seizures begin in both hemispheres
Generalized seizures begin in one area

explanation: Focal seizures start in one area of one hemisphere and can secondarily generalize. Generalized seizures start in both hemispheres.

stem: A 30-year-old man is brought in after convulsing for 12 minutes with no return of awareness. Which of the following defines his condition?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, or recurring seizures without regaining consciousness

explanation: Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or recurring seizures without regaining consciousness.

stem: A patient has a transient loss of consciousness. Which of the following lists the four components of a seizure that help distinguish it from syncope and narcolepsy?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Prodrome, loss of consciousness, physical event, postictal state

explanation: The four components are prodrome, loss of consciousness, physical event and postictal state. Their time course helps separate seizure from syncope and narcolepsy.

stem: Which of the following correctly lists the most common causes of seizures in adults and in children?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Adults: tumors, trauma, infections and stroke; children: infections, trauma and congenital defects

explanation: Adult seizures are most often from tumors, trauma, infections and stroke. Childhood seizures are from infections, trauma and congenital defects.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has her second episode of loss of consciousness with convulsive movements. Which of the following tests best detects abnormal cortical electrical activity?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: EEG detects abnormal cortical electrical activity.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has a single seizure, and no identifiable cause is found. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Treat any identifiable underlying cause; most neurologists will not treat after a single unprovoked episode

explanation: After a single unprovoked seizure most neurologists do not treat, but any identifiable cause should be treated.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has her second unprovoked seizure. Evaluation is unremarkable. Which of the following is the best recommendation?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Start antiseizure treatment, because the likelihood of a third seizure is 80–90%

explanation: After a second unprovoked seizure the risk of a third is 80–90%, so treatment is recommended.

stem: A 40-year-old man has a seizure with fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status, and meningitis is confirmed. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Treat the underlying cause (meningitis), since this is a provoked seizure

explanation: A seizure from meningitis, alcohol withdrawal, electrolyte disturbance or fever is provoked, so treat the cause.

stem: A 52-year-old man with focal seizures has fever, a sore throat and an absolute neutrophil count of 400/µL after starting a new antiseizure drug. Which of the following drugs, with its mechanism and adverse effects, best fits?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Ethosuximide; T-type calcium channel blockade; abdominal pain
Lamotrigine; sodium channel blockade; rash only
Valproic acid; GABA enhancement only; weight loss
Carbamazepine; sodium channel blockade; agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia and Stevens-Johnson syndrome

explanation: Carbamazepine blocks sodium channels. Adverse effects include agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and birth defects.

stem: A 45-year-old man on long-term antiseizure therapy has gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, peripheral neuropathy and megaloblastic anemia. Which of the following drugs and mechanisms is most likely?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Phenytoin blocks sodium channels. Adverse effects: peripheral neuropathy, gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, megaloblastic anemia, DRESS, lupus-like syndrome and birth defects.

stem: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of valproic acid?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Blocks sodium channels and T-type calcium channels and inhibits GABA degradation to raise GABA levels
Enhances GABA-A receptor chloride opening only

explanation: Valproic acid blocks sodium and T-type calcium channels and inhibits GABA degradation.

stem: A woman of childbearing age takes valproic acid. Which of the following sets of adverse effects should she be counseled about?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis and neural tube defects

explanation: Valproic acid causes hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis and neural tube defects.

stem: A patient starts a sodium channel-blocking antiseizure drug that must be titrated slowly because of the risk of a life-threatening skin reaction. Which of the following is the drug and the reaction?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)
explanation: Lamotrigine blocks sodium channels and requires slow titration to reduce the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

stem: A 7-year-old child with absence seizures takes ethosuximide. Which of the following correctly states its mechanism and a serious adverse effect?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: T-type calcium channel blockade in thalamic neurons; Stevens-Johnson syndrome

explanation: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons. A serious adverse effect is Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

stem: A survivor of herpes simplex encephalitis has episodes of a burning smell followed by staring and lip smacking. Which of the following is the most likely origin of these seizures?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Uncus of the temporal lobe (olfactory cortex)

explanation: Uncinate seizures arise from the uncus and olfactory cortex of the temporal lobe, a common site of damage after HSV-1 encephalitis.

stem: A 29-year-old man collapses with a generalized seizure after 2 months of headaches and personality change. Biopsy shows fried-egg cells with a chicken-wire capillary pattern. Which of the following best describes the cause of his seizures?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: A structural cause, namely an oligodendroglioma

explanation: The cause is structural (a tumor), the leading adult cause of new seizures, here an oligodendroglioma.

stem: A 6-year-old girl has staring spells that are reproduced by hyperventilation. Which of the following describes the expected findings?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG, brief episodes and no postictal state
Focal temporal spikes and a long postictal state
Normal EEG and long postictal confusion

explanation: Absence seizures show generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges, are provoked by hyperventilation, and have no postictal state.

stem: In a focal motor seizure with Jacksonian march, which of the following best explains the order of spread of contractions?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Spread along the precentral gyrus in the order of the motor homunculus

explanation: Jacksonian march follows the motor homunculus along the precentral gyrus.

stem: A man has a witnessed collapse. Which of the following best supports seizure rather than syncope or narcolepsy?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Bloody saliva from lateral tongue biting, urinary incontinence and postictal confusion lasting 15 to 20 minutes

explanation: Lateral tongue biting (bloody saliva), incontinence and prolonged postictal confusion support a seizure. Syncope features quick recovery and a prodrome of pallor.

stem: Which of the following best describes the general principles of treating epilepsy?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Start several drugs at once at maximum dose

Start one drug at the lowest dose, titrate until seizures are controlled, the maximum dose is reached or side effects are intolerable, then add a second drug if needed, aiming to eliminate seizures with the fewest side effects

explanation: Treatment aims to eliminate seizures with the fewest side effects and the lowest number and dose of drugs. Start with one drug at the lowest dose and titrate, then add a second if needed.
